raw_response.rationale: This mixed-methods study combines a stratified random survey of 520 households across high- and low-income neighborhoods in Accra, 20 key-stakeholder interviews, focus group discussions, field observations, municipal expenditure records, and GIS spatial mapping of cholera cases. Multiple legal and governance mechanisms are co-central to explaining disparities in water and sanitation access (`assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple` = 'multiple'): (1) `eligibility_status_documentation` (the primary utility/municipal exclusion rule: Ghana Water Company refuses to connect households lacking secure land tenure due to eviction/cost-recovery risk, and municipal authorities exclude 'illegal' settlements like Agbogbloshie for fear of legitimizing tenure), (2) `fees_tariffs_subsidies` (pay-as-you-go water standpipe and public toilet fees, cost-recovery constraints, and AMA's failed 2010 tiered fee-based waste registration scheme), (3) `enforcement_sanctions` (the High Court ban outlawing pan latrines—which drove clandestine night-soil dumping into drains—and the 'one house, one toilet' mandate), and (4) `institutional_structure_coordination` (decentralization without fiscal transfers and shortfalls between planned and actual municipal sanitation expenditure). On outcomes (`assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple` = 'multiple'), the survey primarily tabulates household piped-water and in-house toilet coverage (`primary_connection`, Table 1 and Fig. 3) alongside co-central assessments of service continuity, water contamination, and public toilet condition/distance (`effective_access`), household water/sanitation affordability (`economic_access`), and municipal budget execution (`administrative_outcome`), linking these deficits to cholera incidence.
